COUNCIL TAX — Local Government Finance Act 1992 — Section 3 of the Local Government
Finance Act 1992 — the Council Tax (Chargeable Dwellings (Order) 1992 — Corkish v Wright and
Hart [2014] EWHC 237 (Admin) — Daniels (LO) v Aristides [2006] EWHC 3052 (Admin) — McColl v
Subacchi (LO) [2001] HC (RA 2001 342) — the panel determined that there was one hereditament
but two self-contained units, both of which attracted a separate valuation band — appeal dismissed.

DECISION 
 
1. 
The appeal is dismissed. 
 
2. 
The Tribunal finds that the subject property comprised one hereditament but two self-
contained units, both of which had correctly attracted a separate entry in the valuation list. 
 
STATEMENT OF REASONS 
 
Introduction 
 
3. 
This appeal relates to a proposal to merge the two council tax entries at 15A and 17 
Shepherds Lane (the subject property). 
 
4. 
On 15 May 2025, the Appellant served a proposal on the Respondent Listing Officer. In his 
proposal, the Appellant requested a merger of the two entries in the valuation list with effect 
from 27 February 2025. 
 
5. 
On 3 December 2025, after considering the merits of the proposal, the Respondent Listing 
Officer determined that the proposal was not well founded and a decision notice to that effect 
was issued. 
 
6. 
On 30 January 2026, the Appellant filed an appeal with this Tribunal. 
 
7. 
This statement of reasons is not and does not purport to be a full verbatim record of 
proceedings. 
 
Background 
 
8. 
The subject property was constructed in 1881 as a single dwelling. In the 1980s, the property 
was converted into two separate flats. 15A Shepherds Lane, the first floor flat, was entered 
into the valuation list at band B from 1 April 1993. Prior to merging the property, 15A 
Shepherds Lane comprised of three bedrooms, one bathroom, one reception room and one 
kitchen. 17 Shepherds Lane, the ground floor flat, was entered into the valuation list at band 
D from 1 April 1993. Prior to merging the property, 17 Shepherds Lane comprised of two 
bedrooms, one bathroom, one reception room and one kitchen. Following the decision to 
utilise the subject property as one dwelling, the subject property was comprised of three 
bedrooms, two bathrooms, four reception rooms, one kitchen, and one utility room. 
 
9. 
The Appellant initially purchased 15A Shepherds Lane in 1982 with a leasehold interest in 
the property. Subsequently, 17 Shepherds Lane was purchased by the Appellant in 
November 2023, along with the freehold for the entirety of the property.  
 
10. Following the completion of the sale, the Appellant commenced works to merge the two 
separate flats into one dwelling. As part of the works, the Appellant converted the kitchen on 
the first floor into a utility/laundry room and removed the timber infill wall in the entryway for 
15A Shepherds Lane, allowing access to all floors of the property through one entry point. 
 
11. The Listing Officer determined that no change would be made to the valuation list, deeming 
the existing two entries in the list correct on the basis that both 15A Shepherds Lane and 17 
Shepherds Lane remained self-contained units within one hereditament.

Relevant Law 
 
12. Part I of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 (the Act) makes provision for billing 
authorities in England and Wales to levy a tax, known as council tax, in respect of domestic 
hereditaments (“dwellings”) within their area.   
 
13. Section 3 of the Act provides— 
 
3 Meaning of “dwelling” 
 
… 
 
(2) 
Subject to the following provisions of this section, a dwelling is any 
property which— 
 
(a) 
by virtue of the definition of hereditament in section 115(1) of the 
General Rate Act 1967, would have been a hereditament for the 
purposes of that Act if that Act remained in force; and  
 
(b) 
is not for the time being shown or required to be shown in a local 
or a central non-domestic rating list in force at that time; and  
 
(c) 
is not for the time being exempt from local non-domestic rating for 
the purposes of Part III of the Local Government Finance Act 
1988. 
 
14. The definition of dwelling essentially referred back to the definition of a ‘hereditament’ under 
section 115(1) of the General Rate Act 1967, which stated the following:  
 
115 Interpretation  
 
(1) 
In this Act, except where the context otherwise requires, the following 
expressions have the following meanings respectively, that is to say— 
 
… 
 
" hereditament " means property which is or may become liable to 
a rate, being a unit of such property which is, or would fall to be, 
shown as a separate item in the valuation list; 
 
15. The issue of self-contained units was covered in section 3(5) of the 1992 Act and the Council 
Tax (Chargeable Dwellings) Order 1992 (SI No 1992/549), as amended. Articles 2 and 3 of 
the Order specified that:  
 
“2.  ‘single property’ means property which would, apart from this 
Order, be one dwelling within the meaning of section 3 of the 
Act; and “self-contained unit” means a building or part of a 
building which has been constructed or adapted for use as 
separate living accommodation. 
 
3.  
Subject to article 3A where a single property contains more than one 
self-contained unit, for the purposes of Part 1 of the Act, the property

shall be treated as comprising as many dwellings as there are such 
units included in it and each such unit shall be treated as a dwelling.”  
 
 
16. The Appellant, in his bundle, also referred to Article 4 of the 1992 Order, which states:  
 
4 
 
(1) 
Where, subject to article 3C, a multiple property— 
 
(a) 
consists of a single self-contained unit, or such a unit 
together with or containing premises constructed or adapted 
for non-domestic purposes; and 
 
(b) 
is occupied as more than one unit of separate living 
accommodation, 
 
the listing officer, may, if he thinks fit, subject to paragraph (2) below, treat the 
property as one dwelling. 
 
(2) 
In exercising his discretion in paragraph (1) above, the listing officer 
shall have regard to all the circumstances of the case, including the 
extent, if any, to which the parts of the property separately occupied 
have been structurally altered. 
 
17. Relevant to this appeal, Article 2 of the 1992 Order defines a “multiple property” as: 
 
““multiple property” means property which would, apart from this 
Order, be two or more dwellings within the meaning of section 3 of 
the Act” 
 
18. Prior to the hearing, the clerk circulated to the panel and the parties’ copies of the following 
judgments Corkish v Wright and Hart [2014] EWHC 237 (Admin) and Daniels (LO) v Aristides 
[2006] EWHC 3052 (Admin), which was circulated to the panel and the parties by the clerk 
prior to the hearing. 
 
19. The following case law was also referred to by the Respondent, in the evidence and during 
the hearing: 
 
Salisbury v Bunyan [2021] EWHC 3136 (Admin) 
Coleman (LO) v Rotsztein [2003] EWHC 1057 (Admin) 
Batty v Burfoot and Others [1995] RA 299 
McColl v Subacchi (LO) [2001] EWHC 712 (Admin) 
Jorgensen (LO) v Gomperts [2006] EWHC 1885 (Admin)   
Ramdhun v Valuation Tribunal of England [2014] EWHC 946 (Admin) 
 
Appeal to the Tribunal 
 
20. This appeal was made under regulation 10 of the Council Tax (Alteration of Lists and 
Appeals) (England) Regulations 2009 (SI 2009 No 2270). Relevant to this appeal it provides: 
 
10 Disagreement as to proposed alteration

Where the LO has— 
 
(a)

with regulation 9(2), 
 
the proposer or any competent person may appeal to the VTE against the

Discussion 
 
21. Firstly, it was not contended by either party that there was more than one hereditament; both 
15A and 17 Shepherds Lane were in the same rateable occupation. Ms Murray sought to 
defend the entries in the valuation list on the basis that there was one hereditament that 
comprised two self-contained units. The panel was therefore satisfied that it could proceed 
on the basis there was only a single hereditament and that the question to be answered was 
whether that hereditament contained two self-contained units of living accommodation. 
 
22. Having regard to the relevant statutory provisions, the panel considered that the Listing 
Officer was required to treat part of a dwelling as a separate “self-contained unit” where it 
had been adapted for, or was capable of, use as separate living accommodation. The issue 
for determination was therefore whether the subject property was capable of use as two 
separate units of living accommodation. 
 
23. The Listing Officer explained that a self-contained unit would ordinarily include independent 
access, either by way of its own entrance or through a communal area, together with facilities 
for living and sleeping, washing facilities including a toilet, and basic facilities for the 
preparation of food. 
 
24. The panel turned to the High Court judgment of Corkish (LO) v Wright and Hart. In this case, 
Popplewell J derived six principles from former authorities, which have been set out below: 
 
(1) 
The question is whether the effect of the construction or adaptation is 
such as to make the relevant building or part of a building reasonably 
suitable for use as separate living accommodation. I prefer the 
expression “reasonably suitable” for such use to “capable” of such use, 
because it makes clear that what matters is its fitness for that purpose 
by reference to contemporary standards of what is reasonable, not 
merely whether it might conceivably be used for such purpose however 
remote the possibility.  
 
(2) 
The question is to be answered by reference to the physical 
characteristics of the building. This is sometimes referred to as a “bricks 
and mortar test”, but the epithet does not accurately capture the wide 
range of physical characteristics which may be of relevance including 
services and fixtures.  
 

[2026] VTE VT00035328 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
6/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
(3) 
This is an objective test. The test is not concerned with when, how or 
why those characteristics were achieved. The purpose of the 
construction or adaptation is irrelevant. The test is addressed to the 
result of the building work, not the circumstances in which it was carried 
out. Intention is irrelevant.  
 
(4) 
Whether the test is met is a matter of fact and degree for the tribunal.  
 
(5) 
There is a divergence in the authorities as to whether the actual use to 
which the building has been or is being put is capable of being a 
relevant consideration. The decision attaches to the dwelling through 
changes of ownership and use, such that actual use at any given time 
will rarely help to inform the result of applying an objective test based 
on the physical characteristics of the building. I prefer the view that 
actual use may in some cases be of some relevance. If, for example, 
the part of the property has in fact been used, or is being used, for 
occupation by persons who do not form part of a single household with 
those who occupy the remainder of the property, that may be a factor 
which supports a conclusion that its physical characteristics make it 
suitable for such occupation. However actual use is not the test, and 
even in cases where it may be of some relevance it will not usually be a 
factor of significant weight. At most it may reinforce a decision reached 
by reference to the physical characteristics of the building.  
 
(6) 
If what is being considered is part of a building, the physical 
characteristics to be considered include those of the remainder of the 
building as well as the part being considered. Access is one aspect of 
such characteristics. Separate public access may be a pointer to the 
part being separate living accommodation; whereas if access is through 
the remainder of the building this may tell against the part being 
separate living accommodation. In the latter case different weight may 
be attached where access is through the living areas of the remainder 
of the building from the weight to be attached where it is through a 
hallway. But access is not a factor which can be determinative without 
considering the other physical aspects of the building. The weight to be 
attached to it is a matter for the tribunal. 
 
25. Thus, in deciding this appeal, the panel must consider whether the physical characteristics of 
the subject property made it reasonably suitable for use for two separate living units of 
accommodation. 
 
26. With the above considerations in mind, the panel turned to the arguments and evidence 
presented on behalf of the Respondent Listing Officer. It was the view of Ms Murray that 
there had not been any significant alterations to the subject property in order for it to be 
merged into one assessment. In particular, Ms Murray argued that, while the cooker had 
been removed from the former kitchen on the first floor, facilities for basic food preparation 
remained in place, such as countertops and a sink, indicating that 15A Shepherds Lane 
remained a self-contained unit and, therefore its entry could not be merged for the purposes 
of council tax.   
 
27. After considering the representations from the Respondent, the panel then turned to the 
arguments and evidence submitted by the Appellant. The Appellant argued that the intention

D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
7/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
upon purchasing the second flat, 17 Shepherds Lane, was to convert the subject property 
back into a single dwelling as it was now being utilised as one residential unit. The Appellant 
advised the panel that the water accounts for both properties had been combined and that 
the entire property now operated under a single postal address. To facilitate the merger of the 
two properties, the Appellant advised that the cooker and associated wiring had been 
removed from the first-floor kitchen, which was now used as a utility/laundry room.  
 
28. While the panel accepted that the Appellant’s intention and use of the hereditament was as 
one dwelling rather than two self-contained units, it found that, per Corkish v Wright and Hart, 
these factors were not considered as part of the test. The panel had to consider the physical 
characteristics of both 15A and 17 Shepherds Lane at the proposed effective date. On the 
evidence, the panel considered that the subject property was capable of being used as two 
self-contained units, as both parts contained all the essential elements of a habitable space. 
The panel found that there was no internal photographic evidence of the subject property 
provided by either party, and the sole evidence available to it was a proposed plan of 
changes and planning documents from Dartford Council, neither of which were substantial 
enough to demonstrate that the two flats were no longer self-contained. 
 
29. The panel reached this conclusion notwithstanding the absence of an oven. It noted that the 
first-floor flat retained facilities for basic food preparation, including a sink, work surface, and 
an electricity supply capable of supporting domestic appliances. The panel therefore 
considered that the absence of an oven did not materially affect the flat’s suitability for use as 
living accommodation. In Daniels (LO) v Aristides, Davis J had commented that the presence 
of an oven was not a decisive factor at paragraph [27] of the judgment: 
 
27.  The question of whether or not cooking facilities are or are not crucial in 
a context such as the present was discussed in the case of Jorgensen 
v Gomperts … It seems to me that the judge in that case was correct in 
saying it all depends on the particular circumstances of the particular 
case: sometimes it will be of decisive importance perhaps, and 
sometimes it will not be of decisive importance at all.” 
 
30. In addition, the Appellant stated that the timber infill wall separating the entrance hall of 15A 
Shepherds Lane from the adjoining property had been removed. The Appellant advised that 
the removal of this wall created a single point of access serving both parts of the property 
and provided internal access throughout. The Appellant argued that, as a result, the 
properties no longer had separate means of access and could not readily be occupied as 
separate independent living accommodation. 
 
31. The panel had regard to McColl v Subacchi, in which it was held that access arrangements to 
a self-contained unit, whilst a relevant consideration, is not itself determinative. The fact that 
access may be obtained through the main dwelling does not, of itself, deprive 
accommodation of its character as a self-contained unit. Sir Christopher Bellamy at 
paragraph [27] of that judgment commented: 
 
27. …the question of separate access, while a highly material factor, is not 
an essential condition of "separateness" for the purposes of the 
construction of the Order. 
 
32. In view of the case law and the evidence before it, the panel found that access was not an 
issue in this case as 15A Shepherds Lane did not require access through the living area of 

[2026] VTE VT00035328 (CVAD) 
 
D1-LO Decision (v2603) 
8/8 
www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk 
17 Shepherds Lane. To access the unit on the first floor, the panel found that it could be 
accessed through a communal hallway, rather than through a private area that would impact 
the physical enjoyment of the unit. 
 
33. In addition to the physical changes made to the subject property, the Appellant argued that 
the Listing Officer had failed to exercise her discretion under Article 4 of the Council Tax 
(Chargeable Dwellings) Order 1992 to treat the subject property as a single dwelling. The 
panel noted that Article 4 relates to ‘multiple property’ as detailed in paragraph 17 of this 
decision and was not relevant to the case before it.  
 
34. Having regard to the physical characteristics of the subject property as a whole, the panel 
noted that it was possible to access both units via communal areas. The panel also 
determined that someone could quite comfortably reside at either property, as they each had 
all the necessary living facilities for basic food preparation, sleeping, living and bathing; both 
the flats were reasonably suitable for use as separate living accommodation. The panel 
accepted that the cooker had been removed from the kitchen area in the first floor flat and 
the installation points had been removed. However, the panel remained of the opinion that 
the flat provided all the hallmarks of a self-contained unit.  
 
Conclusion 
 
35. In view of the above findings and conclusions, the panel was satisfied that the subject 
property had been correctly assessed as a single hereditament which contained two self-
contained units that were both capable of use as separate living accommodation. 
 
36. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed.   
 
Right of further appeal 
 
37. Any party who is aggrieved at the Tribunal’s decision has a statutory right of further appeal to 
the High Court on a point of law pursuant to Regulation 43 of the Tribunal Procedure 
Regulations. A party does not require permission to appeal from the Tribunal. Any appeal 
must be made directly to the High Court using Form N161 (Appellant’s Notice) within four 
weeks of the date this decision and statement of reasons was issued. 
 
38. Further information regarding this statutory right of further appeal, and the parties’ other 
rights, is contained in the guidance booklet “A guide to tribunal decisions” available on the 
Tribunal’s website at www.valuationtribunal.gov.uk/guidance-booklets/.
